children.value: Styling other people's components

works on elements your module renders. A component from an installed package
renders its own elements, and unless it happens to read a prop called

, giving
it one does nothing.
The compiler catches this rather than letting you find it in the browser:

properties.source:
$ kirana check src
warning[KRN1703] sx-on-external-component: a component from "@base-ui/react"
receives `sx`, which it does not read
  help: spread the compiled props instead: {...props(styles.root, sx)}
properties.html: $ kirana check src warning[KRN1703] sx-on-external-component: a component from "@base-ui/react" receives `sx`, which it does not read help: spread the compiled props instead: {...props(styles.root, sx)}

children.value: props()
compiles the same handles into

, which every
component that spreads its props onto an element will apply:

properties.html: import { css, props as styleProps } from "@kirana-style/core" const styles = { popup: css({ borderRadius: "0.5rem" }) } export function Popup({ sx, ...rest }: { sx?: Sx }) { return <Dialog.Popup {...rest} {...styleProps(styles.popup, sx)} /> }

children.value: The alias
is a convention, not an API:

is a common
identifier, and the alias keeps the import from shadowing a parameter.
The case one module away
The diagnostic also fires when the component that receives

is yours, but it
hands its rest props to an installed component without reading
first:

properties.html: // Menubar.tsx export function MenubarTrigger({ ...props }) { return <Menu.Trigger {...props} /> // `sx` rides along, unread } // page.tsx <MenubarTrigger sx={styles.trigger} /> // reported here

children.value: Take
out of the rest props and apply it:

properties.html: export function MenubarTrigger({ sx, ...props }: { sx?: Sx }) { return <Menu.Trigger {...props} {...styleProps(sx)} /> }

children.value: Components that render something else

Some libraries let you supply the element a part renders as. The classes belong to
whichever element ends up in the DOM, so pass the styles to the part, and let it
merge:

properties.html: <SidebarMenuButton render={<a href="/docs" />} sx={styles.button} />

children.value:
If instead you style the inner element and the outer part also sets classes, the
outer part's classes can be dropped — the part is not merging anything, it is
rendering your element.
When you cannot pass props at all
Two options, in order:
Style it from an ancestor you do render
with

. Contextual styles sit in a
lower layer, so the element's own styles still win.
Global CSS

, scoped by an attribute the library sets. This is the last
resort — it is markup you do not own, and nothing checks it.
